issues.legal_issue: Conversion to Hinduism may be established by bona fide intention expressed through unequivocal conduct, without a formal purification ceremony.
material_facts: The woman was born to Christian parents and had followed the Christian faith before the marriage.
Her parents arranged the marriage, which was performed according to Hindu rites and customary ceremonies in the presence of invited relatives.
After the marriage, she stopped attending church, followed Hindu customs, and was accepted as Hindu by the local Hindu community.
The man participated in the Hindu marriage ceremony, and the children were treated as Hindus.
The courts below found that she had converted to Hinduism before the marriage.
issues.conclusion: The evidence supported the finding that the woman had converted to Hinduism before the marriage; the Court therefore did not need to decide whether a marriage between a Hindu and a Christian who had not converted would be valid.
issues.legal_principle: A person may become Hindu by conversion. Theoretical allegiance or a bare declaration is insufficient, but bona fide intention to convert accompanied by conduct unequivocally expressing that intention may establish conversion; no formal ceremony of purification or expiation is necessary. The Court relied on Muthusami Mudaliar v. Masilamani alias Subramania Mudaliar, I.L.R. 33 Mad. 342, and Goona Durgaprasada Rao v. Goona Sudarasanaswami, I.L.R. (1940) Mad. 653.

predicates.marriage_validity_dispute: The validity of a marriage is challenged on the ground that one person had not converted to the other's faith before the marriage.
predicates.bona_fide_conversion_intent: The person born into another faith genuinely intended to adopt the new faith before the marriage.
predicates.unequivocal_conversion_conduct: The person's conduct, including participation in the marriage rites and subsequent religious practice or community acceptance, unequivocally manifested that intention.

issues.definition: When a marriage-validity dispute concerns conversion, genuine intent together with unequivocal conduct results in conversion before marriage being established.

issues.legal_issue: A law that applies only to persons domiciled in a specified state cannot be relied on when the required domicile is not pleaded and proved.
material_facts: The man had a previous wife who was alive when he married the woman.
The marriage took place outside the state whose bigamy law was invoked, and the couple lived there after the marriage.
The written defence did not plead that the man was domiciled in that state, and the evidence did not establish that domicile.
The man relied on the law's prohibition of a marriage when either person had a living spouse.
issues.conclusion: It was not proved that the man was domiciled in the state at the time of the marriage, so he could not rely on that state's bigamy law to challenge the marriage.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3 and 4(1) of the Madras Hindu (Bigamy Prevention and Divorce) Act, 1949 made the Act applicable to Hindus domiciled in Madras and rendered certain marriages void. The party relying on the Act had to plead and establish the required domicile; the Court found that this had not been done.

rule.if: marriage_validity_dispute and bigamy_law_defense and invoked_law_requires_domicile and domicile_not_pleaded_or_proved

predicates.marriage_validity_dispute: The validity of a marriage is challenged in a proceeding concerning that marriage.
predicates.bigamy_law_defense: A party relies on a rule prohibiting a marriage because one person had a living spouse.
predicates.invoked_law_requires_domicile: The invoked rule applies only when a specified domicile condition is satisfied.
predicates.domicile_not_pleaded_or_proved: The party relying on the rule neither properly pleaded nor established the required domicile.

issues.definition: In a marriage-validity dispute, a bigamy-law defense is unavailable when the invoked rule requires domicile and that domicile is not pleaded or proved.

issues.legal_issue: A child born during a valid marriage is presumed legitimate unless it is established that the spouses had no access when the child could have been begotten.
material_facts: The child was born during the subsistence of the marriage.
The spouses had disputes and were said to be living apart, but they lived in the same village.
The courts below found no evidence establishing that the husband had no access to the wife during the period when the child could have been begotten.
issues.conclusion: The presumption of legitimacy was not displaced, and the child could not be held illegitimate.
issues.legal_principle: Section 112 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 creates a conclusive presumption of legitimacy for a child born during a valid marriage unless it is shown that the spouses had no access to each other at any time when the child could have been begotten. Non-access may be proved by relevant direct or circumstantial evidence, but the proof must be clear and satisfactory. The Court relied on Chilukuri Venkateswarlu v. Chilukuri Venkatanarayana, [1954] S.C.R. 425, Karapaya v. Mayandi, I.L.R. 12 Rang. 243 (P.C.), and Ammathayee v. Kumaresain, [1967] 1 S.C.R. 363.

rule.if: legitimacy_dispute_in_family_property_claim and valid_marriage and child_born_during_marriage and no_access_not_established

predicates.legitimacy_dispute_in_family_property_cl: A child's legitimacy is disputed in a claim concerning family property or status.
predicates.valid_marriage: The child's parents were in a valid marriage.
predicates.child_born_during_marriage: The child was born while that marriage subsisted.
predicates.no_access_not_established: It was not established that the parents had no access to each other at any time when the child could have been begotten.

issues.definition: In a family-property legitimacy dispute, a child born during a valid marriage is presumed legitimate when non-access at the relevant time has not been established.
